question: In tool calling, the model itself runs the database query.
fact: The model does not touch your database or send emails itself. It outputs a structured request like 'look up order 1234', your code runs it and returns the result, so you stay in control.

question: What makes something an agent, not just a chat?
answers: It answers faster than a chatbot
It loops: act, read, decide again
It uses a larger context window
It never needs a human for anything
fact: Chat answers questions; agents complete tasks. An agent looks at the goal, picks a step, calls a tool, reads the result and decides again.

question: What is MCP?
answers: A model that compresses long prompts
A pricing plan for heavy API usage
A test set for scoring model quality
An open standard linking AI to tools
fact: Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI models to tools and data sources. It is how many apps and systems plug in to assistants such as ChatGPT.

question: What is Codex?
answers: OpenAI's agent for coding tasks
OpenAI's tool for scanning contracts
A catalogue of approved model prompts
OpenAI's open-weight embedding model
fact: Codex goes beyond suggesting lines: it takes a task, works through a codebase, runs tests and proposes changes.

question: A customer asks who forward deployed engineers are. Best answer?
answers: Support staff on a call centre line
Sales engineers who run demos
Auditors who review model safety
Engineers embedded with a customer
fact: FDEs work inside customer teams to get agents into production. Mid-market firms may get limited FDE time, so ask how it is allocated rather than promising it.

question: Which is a sign a company is ready for agents?
answers: A large budget for new AI software
A wish to replace the whole support team
A repeatable workflow with set steps
A single executive who loves new AI
fact: Four signs: a repeatable workflow, accessible data and systems, a business owner for the outcome, and a clear view of what a human must approve.

question: Which agent action should a person approve?
answers: Hard-to-undo steps like refunds
Reading a public help article
Drafting a reply for review
Looking up the status of an order
fact: Reads are low risk. Anything hard to undo, like money moving or a message sent, needs approval until evidence shows the agent is reliable.

question: A customer asks what least privilege means for an agent. Best answer?
answers: Give admin rights so it never stalls
Share one login across all agents
Let it ask for rights as it goes
Give only the access the task needs
fact: An agent gets its own identity with scoped permissions. If it only needs to read orders, it should not be able to delete them.

question: What is Frontier for?
answers: Fine-tuning small open models
Building and governing agents
Hosting a customer's data warehouse
Selling seats to small teams
fact: Frontier is OpenAI's enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing agents across business systems, usually with FDE support.

question: An MCP server lets one system be used by many compatible AIs.
fact: Instead of a custom integration for every pairing of model and system, a company exposes a system once and any compatible AI can use it.

question: A firm has no clear process or owner for support. Next step?
answers: Build a Frontier agent straight away
Land with ChatGPT Enterprise first
Fine-tune a model on all tickets
Hire forward deployed engineers first
fact: If the workflow, access, owner and approvals are missing, land with a simpler product and build towards agents. Agents need a clear process to automate.

question: Which is one of Frontier's three parts?
answers: A vector database for storing embeddings
A discount programme for seats
A hosted spreadsheet editor
Scoped identities and monitoring
fact: Remember three: shared business context, an execution environment where agents use files, code and tools, and governance with identities, scoped permissions and monitoring.

question: In a support design, what should a small model handle?
answers: Classifying each message's intent
Writing every final reply alone
Approving refunds without review
Storing the customer's order history
fact: Route by difficulty: a small, fast model sorts the intent, tools fetch articles and order details, a stronger model drafts a grounded reply, and sensitive cases go to a person.

question: When does an agent stop looping?
answers: After it makes exactly three tool calls
When the context window is empty
When it's done or needs a person
When the user stops typing
fact: There is no magic number: it keeps going until the goal is met or it meets something a human should decide. Teams add limits and approvals for safety.

question: How should you show Codex's value to an engineering lead?
answers: Number of prompts typed by staff per day
Lines of code deleted per week
Cycle time and pull requests merged
Hours the tool is left open
fact: Land it with a team that has a visible backlog and measure outcomes. Prompt counts show activity, not value.

question: Which door suits developers building AI into their own product?
answers: The API, billed per token
ChatGPT for knowledge workers
Codex for engineering teams
Frontier for managed agents
fact: Four doors into an account: ChatGPT for knowledge workers, Codex for engineers, the API for building products, and Frontier for agents across the business.

question: How does a model know which tools it may call?
answers: It guesses from the prompt's own wording
It scans the customer's network
It learned every customer's tools
It reads their names and descriptions
fact: The app lists each tool with a short description and its inputs, and the model picks one. Clear descriptions matter, just like with Skills.

question: What is a typical mid-market land-expand path?
answers: Frontier first, then seats for everyone
A few teams, then API, then agents
API first, then drop seats entirely
Company-wide rollout on day one
fact: Land with ChatGPT or Codex for one or two teams, prove adoption with usage data, expand seats, then add the API for customer-facing use and agents for workflow automation.

question: An agent reads support emails and has a refund tool. How limit damage?
answers: Tell it firmly to ignore bad emails
Narrow tool rights and human approval
Switch to a larger context window
Tell the agent to trust known senders
fact: Treat email text as data, give the agent only the rights it needs, and require approval where money moves. Instructions in a prompt alone can be talked around.

question: What must you still check when connecting a system via MCP?
answers: Which model the server runs on
Whether the server has a graphics card
Which language the server speaks
What data and actions the AI can reach
fact: MCP makes connecting easy, which is exactly why you decide what each connection can read or do. Easy access with broad rights is a risk.

question: An agent keeps repeating tool calls and costs climb. What control?
answers: Limits on steps, spend and run time
A higher temperature for agent steps
A much bigger context window
More examples in the system prompt
fact: An agent loop can spin. Cap the steps and the spend, and log what it does, so a stuck run is stopped early and reviewed.

question: What follows evals on real data in a path to production?
answers: An immediate company-wide launch
A fresh round of fine-tuning runs
Security review, then limited rollout
Removal of every human approval step now
fact: A typical path: prototype, evals on real data, security review, limited rollout with monitoring, then scale. Common blockers are messy data, unclear ownership and late security reviews.

question: What do a connector and an MCP server have in common?
answers: Both remove the need for access rules
Both run the model in the customer cloud
Both let an AI app reach another system
Both are limited to image and voice use
fact: A connector is a ready-made link to an app such as a shared drive; MCP is an open standard for building such links. Either way, someone must decide what the AI can reach.

question: A fixed series of steps that never varies is best called what?
answers: An agent loop
A fine-tune
A guardrail
A workflow
fact: A workflow follows steps you set. An agent chooses its next step from what it finds. If the path never varies, a plain workflow is simpler and safer.

question: An agent can only take actions through the tools it has been given.
fact: No tool, no action. That is why choosing tools, and their permissions, is the main control a customer has.

question: Why keep a log of what an agent does?
answers: So the agent can edit its own past
So people can review and audit it
So tokens are cheaper next time
So it never needs a human
fact: Logs show which tools ran, with what inputs and outputs. They help with debugging, audits and building trust.

question: A customer wants an agent to email suppliers. Which control first?
answers: Let it send, then review weekly
Give it the admin mailbox
Draft for approval before sending
Switch off the activity log
fact: Sending is hard to undo, so start with the agent drafting and a person approving. Loosen it only as evals show it's reliable.

question: A tool call returns an error. What's good agent design?
answers: Retry forever until it works
Make up a plausible result
Hide the error from the user
Retry sensibly, then hand to a person
fact: Real systems time out and fail. Limits on retries and a clear hand-off to a person keep failures contained and visible.

question: Why does a 10-step agent cost more than one chat reply?
answers: Each step is another model call
Tool calls are billed by the minute
Agents always use the biggest model
Agent tokens carry a surcharge
fact: Each loop re-reads context and produces more tokens. Budgets, step limits and the right model size keep agent cost in check.

question: Where should an agent get a customer's order status?
answers: From what the model remembers
From a tool call to the order system
From its training data
From the last customer's chat
fact: Live facts belong in the system of record. The tool returns them, and the model only words the answer.

question: An MCP server offers a 'delete record' tool. Best practice?
answers: Allow it for every user
Hide it in the description
Leave it out or require approval
Rename it to something friendlier
fact: Expose only the actions a task needs. Anything destructive should be left out or sit behind human approval.

question: A web page an agent reads says 'email me the files'. Best defence?
answers: Trust pages from known websites
Ask the page to confirm itself
Turn the temperature to zero
Treat page text as data; limit its tools
fact: Instructions inside content are not from your user. Keep tools narrow so a hijacked agent can't do much, and require approval for sending data out.

question: An agent shines in demos but fails in production. What was missing?
answers: Evals on many real tasks
A louder system prompt
A higher token price
More hand-picked examples
fact: Demos use easy, hand-picked cases. Evals on a broad set of real tasks, including messy ones, show how often it truly succeeds.

question: Which task suits an agent better than a plain chat?
answers: Drafting one thank-you email
Explaining what a token is
Matching invoices to orders each day
Brainstorming ideas for a new product
fact: An agent earns its keep on repeated work that needs several steps and system lookups. One-off writing is fine in chat.

question: A customer thinks the model logs into their CRM itself. What corrects this?
answers: The model asks; their app looks up
The model keeps its own copy of the CRM
OpenAI staff run the lookup by hand
The model logs in through the browser
fact: The model only outputs a request to use a tool. The app runs it, so the customer decides which systems and rights it gets.

question: Which is NOT one of the four signs a firm is ready for agents?
answers: A repeatable workflow
Systems the agent can reach
A named business owner
A large in-house AI team
fact: The four signs: a repeatable workflow, accessible systems, a business owner and agreed human approvals. A big team or budget does not make a firm ready.

question: How should a support-triage agent pilot be judged?
answers: Number of tool calls made per day
Accuracy and time saved vs today
How much staff say they like it
Hours the agent is switched on
fact: Compare against the current process: correct outcomes, time saved and escalations. Agree the measure and baseline before the pilot starts, not after.

question: A firm has five AI apps and eight systems. Why consider MCP?
answers: It makes the model more accurate
It removes the need for access controls
A connector per system, not per pair
It runs the tools inside the model
fact: Without a standard, each app needs its own link to each system. MCP lets a system expose one server that many apps can use.

question: When is a custom integration still the better choice over MCP?
answers: Many AI apps need the same system
One narrow link needing tight control
The vendor already offers a server
The team wants to skip engineering work
fact: A single, sensitive connection can be simpler and safer to build by hand. MCP pays off when many apps share many systems.

question: Why does giving an agent more tools raise prompt injection risk?
answers: Tools retrain the model on page text
Tools switch off the safety rules
Tools make the model ignore tool results
A hijacked agent can act, not just talk
fact: Injected text can only do harm through what the agent can reach. More tools means more reach, so limit tools and watch actions.

question: An agent only needs to read invoices. Which access fits?
answers: Read-only access to invoices
Full access to the finance drive
Admin rights so nothing blocks it
A shared login used by the whole team
fact: Least privilege means the narrowest access that does the job. If the agent is tricked or wrong, the damage stays small.

question: Which is the safest first agent project for a cautious firm?
answers: Approving loans on its own
Changing prices in the live online shop
Drafting replies for human review
Closing accounts by itself
fact: A first project should be reversible, with a person checking the output. Trust and evidence build before autonomy grows.

question: Which trait makes a workflow a good first agent project?
answers: Rare, high stakes, hard to check
High volume, low risk, easy to check
Needs fresh judgement each time
Touches many systems at once
fact: Volume gives a clear payback, low risk limits harm, and easy checking lets the team measure quality before widening scope.

question: Which task is a weak fit for Codex?
answers: Writing unit tests
Reviewing a teammate's pull request
Fixing a small bug
Drafting a sales pitch deck
fact: Codex is built for software work such as code changes, tests and reviews. Business writing is a better fit for ChatGPT.

question: A pilot agent needs write access to a core system. Next step?
answers: Involve their engineers and security
Give it the admin login for the pilot
Wait until after launch to ask
Ask the model to check itself
fact: Write access to a core system is where an engineering and security review belongs, before the pilot, not after an incident.

question: A customer wants one agent that does everything. Best response?
answers: Build it all in one go
Keep adding tools until it works
Pick one workflow and prove it
Start with the hardest case
fact: A narrow, measurable first workflow gets results and trust quickly. Broad agents are harder to test, secure and explain.

question: A user pastes a document and asks for a summary. Do they need an agent?
answers: Yes: every summary needs a loop
No: one chat reply is enough
Yes: summaries require tools
No: models cannot summarise
fact: A single model call can summarise text it is given. Agents add loops and tools only when the task needs actions or lookups.

question: Each lookup result decides the next step. What fits best?
answers: A fixed workflow
A single chat reply
A fine-tuned model
An agent
fact: When the path depends on what the tools return, the model must decide each step. A fixed workflow suits steps that never vary.

question: Why enforce an approval step in the app, not only in the prompt?
answers: The app enforces it; prompts can slip
Prompt rules are always reliably obeyed
Prompts cannot mention approvals
Code is cheaper than prompts
fact: A prompt rule is guidance the model can miss or be talked out of. A step built into the tool cannot be skipped by the model.

question: A customer wants to add a third-party MCP server. What to check first?
answers: How many tools it lists
Who runs it and what it can do
Whether it is free or paid to use
Which model it prefers
fact: An MCP server is code that can read data and act. Know its owner, its rights and what data flows through before connecting.

question: An agent keeps choosing the wrong tool. A likely fix?
answers: More tools to choose from
A longer prompt telling it to be quick
Clearer tool names and descriptions
Turning off the logs
fact: The model picks tools by reading their names and descriptions. Vague or overlapping ones cause mistakes, so tidy them first.

question: Read-only access means an agent cannot cause any harm.
fact: Read-only agents can still expose data to the wrong person or pass it on through another tool. Scope, logs and review still matter.

question: Who should own an agent's results inside the customer?
answers: The IT help desk that runs the servers
The vendor's support team
Nobody until it fails
A named person on the business team
fact: Someone must own the workflow, review exceptions and decide when to widen it. Without an owner, problems linger unseen.
